items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A base that dissolves in water, giving a solution with pH greater than 7"?
items.answer: alkali
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of alkali.

items.stem: "Alkalis are safe because they are the opposite of acids." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Strong alkalis such as sodium hydroxide are corrosive and can damage skin and eyes even more than many acids.
items.markingKey: Strong alkalis such as sodium hydroxide are corrosive and can damage skin and eyes even more than many acids. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an acid and an alkali.
items.answer: An acid has pH below 7 and turns blue litmus red; an alkali has pH above 7, turns red litmus blue and is a soluble base.
items.markingKey: An acid has pH below 7 and turns blue litmus red; an alkali has pH above 7, turns red litmus blue and is a soluble base. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Ingrid measured the pH of a lemon juice sample diluted with different volumes of water (three readings with a pH meter).

Volume of water added / cm³ | pH: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 2.4 | 2.4 | 2.5
10 | 2.9 | 3.0 | 3.0
50 | 3.2 | 3.2 | 3.2
100 | 3.4 | 3.4 | 3.5
500 | 3.7 | 3.9 | 3.7

Calculate the mean pH when the volume of water added was 500 cm³.
items.markingKey: M1 (3.7 + 3.9 + 3.7) ÷ 3; A1 3.77 (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the concentration of an everyday acid (vinegar) affects the time to dissolve an eggshell piece, state the dependent variable and describe how Kwame should measure it.
items.answer: time for a 1 cm² eggshell piece to stop fizzing
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: time for a 1 cm² eggshell piece to stop fizzing.

items.stem: Sana investigated how the concentration of an everyday acid (vinegar) affects the time to dissolve an eggshell piece. The method had this weakness: eggshell pieces had different amounts of membrane attached. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: remove the inner membrane and cut pieces with a template
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: remove the inner membrane and cut pieces with a template

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "hazard symbol"?
options: A pictogram warning of the danger of a substance
A mixture of indicators that shows a range of colours for pH 0–14
Adding powdered limestone or lime to lakes or soils to neutralise acidity
A gas produced when fuels containing sulfur burn; it forms sulfuric acid in rain
items.answer: A pictogram warning of the danger of a substance
items.markingKey: A. "hazard symbol" is a pictogram warning of the danger of a substance.

items.stem: Briefly explain why you should never taste substances in the laboratory to see if they are acidic.
items.answer: Many are toxic or corrosive; indicators give a safe way to test.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many are toxic or corrosive; indicators give a safe way to test. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why lemon juice and vinegar are safe to eat even though they are acids.
items.answer: They are weak and dilute acids, so they do not damage tissues in small amounts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are weak and dilute acids, so they do not damage tissues in small amounts. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "All acids are dangerous and burn skin." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many acids are weak and safe in food (citric acid, ethanoic acid); only strong, concentrated acids are corrosive.
items.markingKey: Many acids are weak and safe in food (citric acid, ethanoic acid); only strong, concentrated acids are corrosive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A bottle in the prep room has lost its label. Describe how you would safely find out if it is acidic, neutral or alkaline, and what safety precautions you would take.
items.answer: Wear eye protection and gloves; treat it as hazardous; use a dropper to put one drop on universal indicator paper on a white tile or add a few drops of universal indicator to a small sample; compare colour with chart: red/orange/yellow acidic, green neutral, blue/purple alkaline; never smell directly or taste; wash spills with water; label once identified.
items.markingKey: Wear eye protection and gloves; treat it as hazardous; use a dropper to put one drop on universal indicator paper on a white tile or add a few drops of universal indicator to a small sample; compare colour with chart: red/orange/yellow acidic, green neutral, blue/purple alkaline; never smell directly or taste; wash spills with water; label once identified.

items.stem: What colour does phenolphthalein turn in an alkali?
items.answer: Pink
items.markingKey: Pink. It is colourless in acid.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a concentrated acid and a strong acid.
items.answer: A strong acid has a very low pH because it releases many H⁺ ions; a concentrated acid has a lot of acid dissolved in a small volume of water.
items.markingKey: A strong acid has a very low pH because it releases many H⁺ ions; a concentrated acid has a lot of acid dissolved in a small volume of water. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why red cabbage juice can be used as an indicator.
items.answer: It contains pigments that change colour depending on pH – red in acid, purple in neutral and green/yellow in alkali. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It contains pigments that change colour depending on pH – red in acid, purple in neutral and green/yellow in alkali. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "pH 6 is more acidic than pH 2." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Lower pH means more acidic; pH 2 is much more acidic than pH 6.
items.markingKey: Lower pH means more acidic; pH 2 is much more acidic than pH 6. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Hydrangea flowers shows natural indicators.
items.answer: Hydrangea flowers are blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil because the availability of aluminium ions changes with pH. Gardeners can change flower colour by changing soil pH.
items.markingKey: Context (Hydrangea flowers are blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil because the availability of aluminium ions changes with pH.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Gardeners can change flower colour by changing soil pH. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to natural indicators.

items.stem:
Lukas predicts the outcome of an investigation into how the pH of a solution affects the colour of a homemade beetroot indicator.
(a) Formulate a hypothesis that includes a scientific explanation. [2]
(b) Identify the independent and dependent variables. [2]
(c) State two variables that must be controlled. [1]
(d) Sketch the shape of the graph you would expect if the hypothesis is correct and explain how it would support the hypothesis. [1]
items.answer: (a) If the pH increases, then the beetroot indicator will change from red to purple to yellow, because its pigments change structure in different pH conditions. (b) IV: pH of buffer solutions (2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12); DV: colour of the indicator recorded against a colour chart (or absorbance with a colorimeter). (c) volume of indicator added (5 drops); the same batch of indicator. (d) A graph of the DV against the IV showing the predicted trend; if the data follow this trend within the spread of repeats, the hypothesis is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 testable prediction; 1 scientific reasoning: If the pH increases, then the beetroot indicator will change from red to purple to yellow, because its pigments change structure in different pH conditions. (b) 1 IV: pH of buffer solutions (2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12); 1 DV: colour of the indicator recorded against a colour chart (or absorbance with a colorimeter). (c) 1 any two of volume of indicator added (5 drops) (more indicator gives deeper colour); volume of buffer (2 cm³) (affects concentration); white background and lighting (affects how colour is seen); the same batch of indicator (batches differ in strength). (d) 1 graph shape consistent with the hypothesis, linked to support.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the pH of a solution affects the colour of a homemade beetroot indicator. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Prepare beetroot juice by boiling and filtering; put 2 cm³ of each buffer in wells of a white spotting tile; add 5 drops of indicator; record the colour; repeat three times; compare with universal indicator colours.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (buffers at pH 2 and 12 are irritants – wear eye protection; hot liquid when boiling beetroot). Model: Prepare beetroot juice by boiling and filtering; put 2 cm³ of each buffer in wells of a white spotting tile; add 5 drops of indicator; record the colour; repeat three times; compare with universal indicator colours.

items.stem: "Universal indicator is good enough for all pH measurements in school." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Universal indicator is fine for approximate pH; pH meters are needed for accurate work.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cheap, quick, shows approximate pH. Arguments against: colour judgement is subjective; cannot be used with coloured solutions; only to nearest whole number. Supported judgement: Universal indicator is fine for approximate pH; pH meters are needed for accurate work. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "litmus"?
options: Adding powdered limestone or lime to lakes or soils to neutralise acidity
An indicator that is red in acid and blue in alkali
A salt made from hydrochloric acid
A method of adding one solution to another to find the exact volume needed for neutralisation
items.answer: An indicator that is red in acid and blue in alkali
items.markingKey: B. "litmus" is an indicator that is red in acid and blue in alkali.

items.stem: Briefly explain why litmus cannot tell you how strong an acid is.
items.answer: It only has two colours (red in acid, blue in alkali); it shows whether a solution is acidic but not the pH value.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It only has two colours (red in acid, blue in alkali); it shows whether a solution is acidic but not the pH value. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a concentrated acid and a strong acid.
items.answer: A strong acid has a very low pH because it releases many H⁺ ions; a concentrated acid has a lot of acid dissolved in a small volume of water.
items.markingKey: A strong acid has a very low pH because it releases many H⁺ ions; a concentrated acid has a lot of acid dissolved in a small volume of water. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "The pH scale only goes from 1 to 10." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The usual pH scale runs from 0 to 14.
items.markingKey: The usual pH scale runs from 0 to 14. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Jonas measured the pH of soil samples taken at different distances from a limestone footpath (three samples at each distance).

Distance from path / m | Soil pH: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 8.0 | 7.4 | 7.6
5 | 7.6 | 7.5 | 5.0
10 | 7.0 | 6.9 | 7.2
20 | 5.9 | 6.4 | 6.1
40 | 5.8 | 5.6 | 5.8

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean soil pH at 5 m, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 5.0 (trial 3 at 5 m); mean = 7.55
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (5.0) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 7.55.

items.stem:
Tomás measured the pH of soil samples taken at different distances from a limestone footpath (three samples at each distance).

Distance from path / m | Soil pH: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 8.7 | 8.4 | 8.5
5 | 8.5 | 8.3 | 8.5
10 | 7.8 | 7.8 | 7.7
20 | 6.7 | 7.0 | 7.1
40 | 6.4 | 6.3 | 6.4

State the distance from path at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 20 m; range = 0.4; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 20 m; 1 range = max − min = 7.1 − 6.7 = 0.4; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Describe how to make an indicator from red cabbage and test whether it can distinguish between acids and alkalis. Include a fair-test plan.
items.answer: Chop red cabbage, boil or soak in hot water, filter to obtain purple juice. Add the same volume (5 drops) to 2 cm³ of solutions of known pH (e.g. pH 1, 4, 7, 10, 13) on a spotting tile; record colours to make a colour chart; then test unknown solutions and compare. Control volume of indicator and sample; use a white background; compare with universal indicator or pH meter.
items.markingKey: Chop red cabbage, boil or soak in hot water, filter to obtain purple juice. Add the same volume (5 drops) to 2 cm³ of solutions of known pH (e.g. pH 1, 4, 7, 10, 13) on a spotting tile; record colours to make a colour chart; then test unknown solutions and compare. Control volume of indicator and sample; use a white background; compare with universal indicator or pH meter.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A method of adding one solution to another to find the exact volume needed for neutralisation"?
items.answer: titration
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of titration.

items.stem: A student claims: "Neutralisation always gives a solution with pH 7." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only if exactly the right amounts react; excess acid or alkali leaves the pH below or above 7.
items.markingKey: Only if exactly the right amounts react; excess acid or alkali leaves the pH below or above 7. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between reacting an acid with a carbonate and reacting an acid with an alkali.
items.answer: Acid + alkali gives a salt and water only; acid + carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide (fizzing).
items.markingKey: Acid + alkali gives a salt and water only; acid + carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide (fizzing). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Maya measured the volume of 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid needed to neutralise 25 cm³ of different antacid solutions (three titrations each).

Mass of antacid dissolved / g | Volume of acid / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 3.8 | 3.7 | 3.7
0.2 | 7.4 | 7.4 | 7.1
0.3 | 11.2 | 11.2 | 11.5
0.4 | 14.8 | 14.3 | 15.2
0.5 | 18.7 | 17.9 | 18.3

Calculate the mean volume of acid when the mass of antacid dissolved was 0.1 g.
items.answer: 3.73 cm³
items.markingKey: M1 (3.8 + 3.7 + 3.7) ÷ 3; A1 3.73 cm³ (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Antacid tablets shows neutralisation in medicine.
items.answer: Tablets containing magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate neutralise excess stomach acid that causes indigestion and heartburn. A simple reaction relieves a common problem; overuse can affect the body’s mineral balance.
items.markingKey: Context (Tablets containing magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate neutralise excess stomach acid that causes indigestion and heartburn.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A simple reaction relieves a common problem; overuse can affect the body’s mineral balance. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to neutralisation in medicine.

items.stem: 10 cm³ of sodium hydroxide of concentration 1 mol/dm³ is neutralised by hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.2 mol/dm³. The acid and alkali react 1 : 1. What volume of acid is needed?
items.answer: 50 cm³
items.markingKey: M1 equal amounts react: 10 × 1 = V × 0.2; M1 V = 10 × 1 ÷ 0.2; A1 50 cm³.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the volume of sodium hydroxide added affects the temperature of hydrochloric acid during neutralisation. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Put 25 cm³ of acid in a polystyrene cup with a lid; record temperature; add sodium hydroxide 5 cm³ at a time from a burette, stirring; record the temperature after each addition; continue to 40 cm³; repeat; plot temperature against volume and find the maximum.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (sodium hydroxide is corrosive – wear eye protection and gloves). Model: Put 25 cm³ of acid in a polystyrene cup with a lid; record temperature; add sodium hydroxide 5 cm³ at a time from a burette, stirring; record the temperature after each addition; continue to 40 cm³; repeat; plot temperature against volume and find the maximum.

items.stem: "Antacids are a good long-term treatment for heartburn." Discuss.
items.answer: Antacids are fine for occasional heartburn, but frequent symptoms need medical advice and lifestyle changes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: quick relief by neutralising acid; cheap and available. Arguments against: treat symptoms, not causes (diet, weight, smoking); long-term use may mask serious conditions. Supported judgement: Antacids are fine for occasional heartburn, but frequent symptoms need medical advice and lifestyle changes. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "sulfate".
items.answer: A salt made from sulfuric acid
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a salt made from sulfuric acid. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the temperature rises during neutralisation.
items.answer: Neutralisation is exothermic – energy is released when H⁺ and OH⁻ ions combine to form water.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Neutralisation is exothermic – energy is released when H⁺ and OH⁻ ions combine to form water. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why indicator is used in a titration.
items.answer: Acid and alkali solutions are both colourless, so the indicator shows the exact point when the acid is neutralised.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Acid and alkali solutions are both colourless, so the indicator shows the exact point when the acid is neutralised. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Alessia plans to investigate how the volume of sodium hydroxide added affects the temperature of hydrochloric acid during neutralisation. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: volume and concentration of acid (25 cm³); concentration of alkali; insulated polystyrene cup with lid; stirring after each addition
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: volume and concentration of acid (25 cm³) – more acid reacts with more alkali; concentration of alkali – affects the volume needed; insulated polystyrene cup with lid – reduces heat loss; stirring after each addition – mixes evenly. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: In a titration, the volumes of acid needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of alkali were 10.00, 10.10 and 10.10 cm³. Calculate the mean volume.
Noah writes: "Neutralisation always gives a solution with pH 7." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Only if exactly the right amounts react; excess acid or alkali leaves the pH below or above 7.
items.markingKey: Only if exactly the right amounts react; excess acid or alkali leaves the pH below or above 7. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe how to prepare pure, dry crystals of copper chloride from copper oxide and an acid. Name the acid and write the word equation.
items.answer: Warm dilute hydrochloric acid; add copper oxide a spatula at a time with stirring until some remains unreacted (excess); filter to remove unreacted copper oxide; heat filtrate gently to evaporate some water until crystals start to form; leave to cool and crystallise; filter and dry crystals between filter paper. copper oxide + hydrochloric acid → copper chloride + water.
items.markingKey: Warm dilute hydrochloric acid; add copper oxide a spatula at a time with stirring until some remains unreacted (excess); filter to remove unreacted copper oxide; heat filtrate gently to evaporate some water until crystals start to form; leave to cool and crystallise; filter and dry crystals between filter paper. copper oxide + hydrochloric acid → copper chloride + water.

items.stem: Why do farmers spread lime on fields?
items.answer: To neutralise acidic soil
items.markingKey: To neutralise acidic soil. Crops grow poorly in acid soil.

items.stem: "Normal rain is neutral (pH 7)." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Normal rain is slightly acidic (about pH 5.6) because carbon dioxide dissolves in it; acid rain is more acidic than this.
items.markingKey: Normal rain is slightly acidic (about pH 5.6) because carbon dioxide dissolves in it; acid rain is more acidic than this. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Acid rain in Scandinavia and the 1979 Geneva Convention shows international action on pollution.
items.answer: Lakes in Norway and Sweden lost fish populations because of acid rain from pollution produced in other countries; this led to an international agreement to cut sulfur emissions. Sulfur dioxide emissions in Europe fell by over 80% and many lakes have started to recover.
items.markingKey: Context (Lakes in Norway and Sweden lost fish populations because of acid rain from pollution produced in other countries; this led to an international agreement to cut sulfur emissions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Sulfur dioxide emissions in Europe fell by over 80% and many lakes have started to recover. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to international action on pollution.

items.stem:
Alessia placed equal-sized marble chips in sulfuric acid solutions of different pH for one week and measured the percentage mass lost.

pH of solution | Mass lost / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 8.6 | 8.5 | 8.2
3 | 4.5 | 4.7 | 4.5
4 | 2.9 | 3.1 | 2.9
5 | 2.1 | 2.2 | 2.2
6 | 1.6 | 1.6 | 1.7

Calculate the mean mass lost when the pH of solution was 2.
items.markingKey: M1 (8.6 + 8.5 + 8.2) ÷ 3; A1 8.43 % (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Explain how acid rain forms, describe two of its effects, and evaluate two ways of reducing it.
items.answer: Burning fossil fuels with sulfur produces SO₂; high-temperature engines produce NOx; these dissolve in water in clouds forming sulfuric and nitric acid. Effects: kills fish and trees, damages limestone buildings and metal structures. Reduce: flue gas desulfurisation (effective but costly), catalytic converters (reduce NOx from cars), low-sulfur fuels, renewable energy (removes the cause). Liming lakes treats symptoms only.
items.markingKey: Burning fossil fuels with sulfur produces SO₂; high-temperature engines produce NOx; these dissolve in water in clouds forming sulfuric and nitric acid. Effects: kills fish and trees, damages limestone buildings and metal structures. Reduce: flue gas desulfurisation (effective but costly), catalytic converters (reduce NOx from cars), low-sulfur fuels, renewable energy (removes the cause). Liming lakes treats symptoms only.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Removing sulfur dioxide from power station waste gases using a base such as calcium carbonate"?
items.answer: flue gas desulfurisation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of flue gas desulfurisation.

items.stem: Explain why acid rain can kill fish in lakes.
items.answer: The lake becomes more acidic; low pH damages fish gills and eggs and releases toxic aluminium ions from soil into the water.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The lake becomes more acidic; low pH damages fish gills and eggs and releases toxic aluminium ions from soil into the water. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ana is investigating how the pH of simulated acid rain affects the germination of cress seeds. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the pH is lower, then fewer seeds will germinate, because acidic conditions damage enzymes and cell membranes in the seeds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the pH is lower, then fewer seeds will germinate, because acidic conditions damage enzymes and cell membranes in the seeds.

items.stem: Elena investigated how the pH of simulated acid rain affects the germination of cress seeds. The method had this weakness: the pH of the solutions was not checked. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: measure each solution’s pH with a calibrated pH meter before use
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: measure each solution’s pH with a calibrated pH meter before use

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A mixture of indicators that shows a range of colours for pH 0–14"?
items.answer: universal indicator
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of universal indicator.

items.stem: What pH is a solution when an acid has been exactly neutralised by an alkali?
items.markingKey: D. Neutral.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "alkali".
items.answer: A base that dissolves in water, giving a solution with pH greater than 7
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a base that dissolves in water, giving a solution with pH greater than 7. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the causes of global warming and the causes of acid rain.
items.answer: Acid rain is caused mainly by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides forming acids; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trapping heat.
items.markingKey: Acid rain is caused mainly by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides forming acids; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trapping heat. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between universal indicator and litmus.
items.answer: Litmus shows only acid (red) or alkali (blue); universal indicator shows a range of colours that give an approximate pH.
items.markingKey: Litmus shows only acid (red) or alkali (blue); universal indicator shows a range of colours that give an approximate pH. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a chloride and a sulfate.
items.answer: A chloride is a salt made from hydrochloric acid (e.g. NaCl); a sulfate is a salt made from sulfuric acid (e.g. CuSO₄).
items.markingKey: A chloride is a salt made from hydrochloric acid (e.g. NaCl); a sulfate is a salt made from sulfuric acid (e.g. CuSO₄). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between an alkali and a base.
items.answer: A base is any substance that neutralises an acid; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
items.markingKey: A base is any substance that neutralises an acid; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why catalytic converters reduce acid rain.
items.answer: They convert nitrogen oxides from car exhausts into harmless nitrogen and oxygen before they leave the exhaust.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They convert nitrogen oxides from car exhausts into harmless nitrogen and oxygen before they leave the exhaust. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Rafael writes: "The pH scale only goes from 1 to 10." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The usual pH scale runs from 0 to 14.
items.markingKey: The usual pH scale runs from 0 to 14. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Elena is investigating how the volume of sodium hydroxide added affects the temperature of hydrochloric acid during neutralisation. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If more alkali is added, then the temperature will rise until the acid is neutralised and then fall, because neutralisation is exothermic and extra alkali only cools the mixture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If more alkali is added, then the temperature will rise until the acid is neutralised and then fall, because neutralisation is exothermic and extra alkali only cools the mixture.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the concentration of an everyday acid (vinegar) affects the time to dissolve an eggshell piece, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: volume of vinegar (20 cm³).
items.answer: more acid reacts longer
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (volume of vinegar (20 cm³)) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: more acid reacts longer. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: A farmer needs 2 tonnes of lime per hectare to raise the pH of a field from 5.5 to 6.5. The field is 2 hectares. How much lime is needed, and why does raising the pH help crops?
items.answer: 4 tonnes; most crops grow best in near-neutral soil where nutrients are more available
items.markingKey: M1 2 × 2; A1 4 tonnes; B1 neutralises soil acid / nutrients more available.

items.stem: Sana plans to investigate how the pH of a solution affects the colour of a homemade beetroot indicator. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: volume of indicator added (5 drops); volume of buffer (2 cm³); white background and lighting; the same batch of indicator
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: volume of indicator added (5 drops) – more indicator gives deeper colour; volume of buffer (2 cm³) – affects concentration; white background and lighting – affects how colour is seen; the same batch of indicator – batches differ in strength. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: With reference to Antacid tablets, explain how it illustrates neutralisation in medicine.
items.answer: Tablets containing magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate neutralise excess stomach acid that causes indigestion and heartburn. A simple reaction relieves a common problem; overuse can affect the body’s mineral balance.
items.markingKey: Context (Tablets containing magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate neutralise excess stomach acid that causes indigestion and heartburn.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A simple reaction relieves a common problem; overuse can affect the body’s mineral balance. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to neutralisation in medicine.

items.stem:
Arjun measured the pH of a lemon juice sample diluted with different volumes of water (three readings with a pH meter).

Volume of water added / cm³ | pH: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 2.4 | 2.4 | 2.2
10 | 2.7 | 2.8 | 2.7
50 | 3.0 | 2.9 | 2.9
100 | 3.1 | 3.2 | 3.1
500 | 3.5 | 3.5 | 3.7

Calculate the percentage change in the mean pH between 0 cm³ and 500 cm³.
items.markingKey: M1 means 2.33 and 3.57; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 +52.9% (increase).

items.stem: Lars wants to find out how the pH of simulated acid rain affects the germination of cress seeds. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does pH of the watering solution affect percentage of 50 seeds that germinate in 5 days?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (pH of the watering solution (3, 4, 5, 6, 7)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (percentage of 50 seeds that germinate in 5 days) in a question form.

items.stem: Yusuf investigated how the pH of a solution affects the colour of a homemade beetroot indicator. The method had this weakness: the colours were judged under a yellow lamp. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: use daylight or a white LED and a white background; or use a colorimeter
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: use daylight or a white LED and a white background; or use a colorimeter

items.stem: Aiko plans an investigation into how the volume of sodium hydroxide added affects the temperature of hydrochloric acid during neutralisation. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (volume of sodium hydroxide added (0 to 40 cm³ in 5 cm³ portions)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: "Household cleaning products containing strong alkalis should only be sold with child-proof caps." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Child-proof caps are justified for corrosive products, along with clear labelling and safe storage.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: prevent accidental poisoning and burns in children; cheap to do. Arguments against: some adults find them hard to open; education and safe storage also needed. Supported judgement: Child-proof caps are justified for corrosive products, along with clear labelling and safe storage. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "International agreements are the most effective way to tackle acid rain." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Agreements were crucial in driving technology and cutting emissions, though they rely on enforcement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: pollution crosses borders, so cooperation is needed; European SO₂ emissions fell sharply after agreements. Arguments against: some countries may not sign or enforce them; technology (desulfurisation, catalytic converters) did the actual reduction. Supported judgement: Agreements were crucial in driving technology and cutting emissions, though they rely on enforcement. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "litmus".
items.answer: An indicator that is red in acid and blue in alkali
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an indicator that is red in acid and blue in alkali. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "sulfate"?
options: A substance with a pH less than 7 that turns blue litmus red
A hazard meaning the substance can cause inflammation or reddening of the skin or eyes
A salt made from nitric acid
A salt made from sulfuric acid
items.answer: A salt made from sulfuric acid
items.markingKey: D. "sulfate" is a salt made from sulfuric acid.

items.stem: Which of these is an everyday acid?
items.answer: Vinegar (ethanoic acid)
items.markingKey: Vinegar (ethanoic acid). Lemon juice and cola are also acidic.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the causes of acid rain and the causes of global warming.
items.answer: Acid rain is caused mainly by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides forming acids; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trapping heat.
items.markingKey: Acid rain is caused mainly by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides forming acids; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trapping heat. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why red cabbage juice can be used as an indicator.
items.answer: It contains pigments that change colour depending on pH – red in acid, purple in neutral and green/yellow in alkali.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It contains pigments that change colour depending on pH – red in acid, purple in neutral and green/yellow in alkali. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a chloride and a sulfate.
items.answer: A chloride is a salt made from hydrochloric acid (e.g. NaCl); a sulfate is a salt made from sulfuric acid (e.g. CuSO₄).
items.markingKey: A chloride is a salt made from hydrochloric acid (e.g. NaCl); a sulfate is a salt made from sulfuric acid (e.g. CuSO₄). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Noah writes: "Alkalis are safe because they are the opposite of acids." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Strong alkalis such as sodium hydroxide are corrosive and can damage skin and eyes even more than many acids.
items.markingKey: Strong alkalis such as sodium hydroxide are corrosive and can damage skin and eyes even more than many acids. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "Normal rain is neutral (pH 7)." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Normal rain is slightly acidic (about pH 5.6) because carbon dioxide dissolves in it; acid rain is more acidic than this.
items.markingKey: Normal rain is slightly acidic (about pH 5.6) because carbon dioxide dissolves in it; acid rain is more acidic than this. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.
items.answer: A strong acid has a very low pH because it releases many H⁺ ions; a concentrated acid has a lot of acid dissolved in a small volume of water.
items.markingKey: A strong acid has a very low pH because it releases many H⁺ ions; a concentrated acid has a lot of acid dissolved in a small volume of water. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Arjun measured the volume of 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid needed to neutralise 25 cm³ of different antacid solutions (three titrations each).

Mass of antacid dissolved / g | Volume of acid / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 4.2 | 4.2 | 4.3
0.2 | 8.3 | 8.4 | 8.7
0.3 | 12.7 | 12.5 | 12.7
0.4 | 17.4 | 16.7 | 17.3
0.5 | 21.0 | 21.3 | 20.4

State the mass of antacid dissolved at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 0.5 g; range = 0.9 cm³; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 0.5 g; 1 range = max − min = 21.3 − 20.4 = 0.9 cm³; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem:
Omar measured the pH of a lemon juice sample diluted with different volumes of water (three readings with a pH meter).

Volume of water added / cm³ | pH: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 2.1 | 2.1 | 2.2
10 | 2.6 | 2.5 | 2.4
50 | 2.8 | 2.8 | 2.9
100 | 3.0 | 2.9 | 2.9
500 | 3.2 | 3.2 | 3.4

Calculate the mean pH when the volume of water added was 0 cm³.
items.markingKey: M1 (2.1 + 2.1 + 2.2) ÷ 3; A1 2.13 (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Using Acid rain in Scandinavia and the 1979 Geneva Convention as an example, explain international action on pollution.
items.answer: Lakes in Norway and Sweden lost fish populations because of acid rain from pollution produced in other countries; this led to an international agreement to cut sulfur emissions. Sulfur dioxide emissions in Europe fell by over 80% and many lakes have started to recover.
items.markingKey: Context (Lakes in Norway and Sweden lost fish populations because of acid rain from pollution produced in other countries; this led to an international agreement to cut sulfur emissions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Sulfur dioxide emissions in Europe fell by over 80% and many lakes have started to recover. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to international action on pollution.

items.stem:
Amara measured the pH of soil samples taken at different distances from a limestone footpath (three samples at each distance).

Distance from path / m | Soil pH: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 6.6 | 6.7 | 6.4
5 | 6.4 | 6.5 | 6.5
10 | 6.1 | 5.8 | 6.2
20 | 5.2 | 5.2 | 5.4
40 | 5.1 | 5.2 | 4.8

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The soil pH decreases (becomes more acidic) with distance from the limestone path. Limestone (calcium carbonate) dust from the path neutralises soil acids nearby, so the soil is less acidic close to the path.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The soil pH decreases (becomes more acidic) with distance from the limestone path.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Limestone (calcium carbonate) dust from the path neutralises soil acids nearby, so the soil is less acidic close to the path.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the volume of sodium hydroxide added affects the temperature of hydrochloric acid during neutralisation, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: insulated polystyrene cup with lid.
items.answer: reduces heat loss
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (insulated polystyrene cup with lid) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: reduces heat loss. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Jonas is investigating how the concentration of an everyday acid (vinegar) affects the time to dissolve an eggshell piece. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: concentration of vinegar (25%, 50%, 75%, 100% diluted with water)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: concentration of vinegar (25%, 50%, 75%, 100% diluted with water) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Mei placed equal-sized marble chips in sulfuric acid solutions of different pH for one week and measured the percentage mass lost.

pH of solution | Mass lost / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 7.5 | 7.3 | 7.9
3 | 4.2 | 4.2 | 4.0
4 | 2.6 | 2.6 | 2.7
5 | 2.0 | 1.9 | 1.9
6 | 1.4 | 1.5 | 1.5

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The percentage mass lost decreases as the pH increases (solution less acidic). Lower pH means a higher concentration of acid, which reacts with the calcium carbonate in marble faster, dissolving more of it.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The percentage mass lost decreases as the pH increases (solution less acidic).; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Lower pH means a higher concentration of acid, which reacts with the calcium carbonate in marble faster, dissolving more of it.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Universal indicator is good enough for all pH measurements in school."
items.answer: Universal indicator is fine for approximate pH; pH meters are needed for accurate work.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cheap, quick, shows approximate pH. Arguments against: colour judgement is subjective; cannot be used with coloured solutions; only to nearest whole number. Supported judgement: Universal indicator is fine for approximate pH; pH meters are needed for accurate work.

items.stem: "Antacids are a good long-term treatment for heartburn." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Antacids are fine for occasional heartburn, but frequent symptoms need medical advice and lifestyle changes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: quick relief by neutralising acid; cheap and available. Arguments against: treat symptoms, not causes (diet, weight, smoking); long-term use may mask serious conditions. Supported judgement: Antacids are fine for occasional heartburn, but frequent symptoms need medical advice and lifestyle changes.
